objectives: State Hubble's law + derive an age estimate from H_0.
Connect CMB observations to early-universe physics.
Explain why BBN + CMB jointly constrain the baryon density.

slides.title: Hubble's law + the expanding universe
slides.body:
Hubble (1929): galaxies' redshifts increase linearly with distance — **v = H_0 d**. The Hubble constant H_0 has units of 1/time. Current best value (2024 consensus): H_0 ≈ 67-74 km/s/Mpc, with a persistent ~5σ **'Hubble tension'** between early-universe (CMB → ~67.4) and late-universe (Cepheid+SNe Ia → ~73.0) measurements.

Naively: t_H = 1/H_0 ≈ 14 Gyr — the Hubble time, a rough age of the universe. ΛCDM + measured composition gives a refined age of **13.79 ± 0.02 Gyr**.

The redshift z = (λ_obs − λ_rest)/λ_rest is **cosmological** — not Doppler. Space itself stretches; photons travelling through it stretch with it. For z ≫ 1, 1 + z = a_now / a_emit (scale factor ratio). At z = 1100 (CMB era): the universe was ~1100× smaller in linear extent.

slides.title: The cosmic microwave background
slides.body:
Predicted by Gamow + Alpher + Herman (1948); discovered by Penzias + Wilson (1965) as an inexplicable 4 K excess noise in a Bell Labs radio antenna. The **CMB** is a 2.725 K thermal blackbody filling all of space; the most perfect blackbody ever observed.

It's the relic radiation from the **recombination** era at t ≈ 380,000 years, z ≈ 1100, when the universe had cooled enough for free electrons + protons to recombine into neutral hydrogen — letting photons stream freely for the first time. The 2.725 K we measure is the redshifted 3000 K thermal field from that moment.

The CMB has tiny anisotropies (ΔT/T ~ 10⁻⁵) carrying enormous information: COBE (1992 Nobel) found them; WMAP + Planck mapped them to exquisite precision. The angular power spectrum has a sequence of **acoustic peaks** whose positions + heights constrain: Ω_total, Ω_b, Ω_m, Ω_Λ, H_0, the scalar spectral index n_s, and more. ΛCDM emerged as the standard model of cosmology mostly from CMB fits.

slides.title: Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN)
slides.body:
Between t ~ 1 second and ~20 minutes, the universe was hot (10⁹ - 10¹⁰ K) + dense enough for nuclear reactions: protons + neutrons fused into light nuclei. By t = 20 min, expansion cooled everything below the fusion threshold; primordial element abundances were locked in.

BBN predicts: **~75% H, ~25% ⁴He** (by mass), plus trace **D (2H), ³He, ⁷Li** at parts per ~10⁵. These are *the* primordial abundances; everything heavier (C, N, O, etc.) was made later in stars + supernovae.

The match between BBN predictions + observed light-element abundances (deuterium especially is a sensitive 'baryometer') gives Ω_b ≈ 0.05 — independently of the CMB. Two completely orthogonal probes (BBN at t ~ 100 s + CMB at t ~ 380 kyr) yield the same baryon density to within ~5%. This is among the cleanest cosmological agreements + a major triumph of the Big Bang model.

**Lithium problem**: predicted ⁷Li is ~3× observed — a persistent ~3σ tension, possibly resolved by stellar destruction or BBN refinements.

slides.title: Derive the age of the universe in a matter-only universe
slides.statement: Assume the universe contains only matter (no Λ, no radiation). The Friedmann equation gives H² = (8πG/3)ρ_m and ρ_m ∝ a⁻³.

steps.prompt: Show H = H_0 (a/a_0)^(−3/2) where a_0 is the current scale factor.
steps.answer: H² ∝ ρ_m ∝ a⁻³, so H ∝ a^(−3/2). Normalizing at today: H = H_0 (a/a_0)^(−3/2).

steps.prompt: With H_0 = 70 km/s/Mpc, convert 1/H_0 to Gyr, then compute t_0 = 2/(3H_0).
The real measured age is ~13.8 Gyr — much closer to 1/H_0 itself than 2/(3 H_0). What's wrong with the matter-only model?
steps.answer: We ignored dark energy (Λ). In ΛCDM, the universe has been *accelerating* for the last ~5 Gyr because Λ drives da/dt up. Including Λ ≈ 0.69, t_0 ≈ 13.8 Gyr — closer to 1/H_0 because acceleration means t_0 > 2/(3 H_0). The fact that the simple matter-only estimate underpredicts age by ~30% was one of the early hints of dark energy (alongside Type Ia SNe at z ~ 1).

slides.prompt: What does the position of the first acoustic peak in the CMB angular power spectrum (~ℓ ≈ 220, ~1° on the sky) primarily measure?

choices.label: The baryon-to-photon ratio η.
choices.rationale: η is constrained mostly by *peak height ratios* (2nd to 1st peak ratio gauges baryon loading), not the first peak's position.

choices.label: The total energy density of the universe, indicating spatial geometry (flat vs curved).
choices.rationale: Correct. The angular size of the sound horizon at recombination is a standard ruler. In a flat universe, it subtends ~1°; in a closed universe it appears larger (peak at smaller ℓ); in an open universe smaller (peak at larger ℓ). Observed first-peak position at ℓ ≈ 220 ⇒ universe is **flat** to within ~0.5% (Ω_total = 1.000 ± 0.005).

choices.label: The mass of the neutrino species.
choices.rationale: Neutrino masses affect structure formation + the damping tail of the CMB, not the first peak's position.

choices.label: The Hubble constant H_0 directly.
choices.rationale: H_0 is constrained by combining CMB peaks with priors / other data (baryon acoustic oscillations, supernovae). The first peak's position alone constrains geometry × distance to last-scattering, not H_0 alone.

slides.hint: Think 'standard ruler' subtending an angle — what determines that angle?
slides.workedSolution: The sound horizon at recombination (~150 Mpc comoving) is the maximum distance acoustic waves in the photon-baryon plasma could have traveled by t = 380 kyr — a calculable physical length. Its angular extent on the sky depends on the cosmic distance to z = 1100, which depends on the universe's spatial curvature. In flat ΛCDM the predicted angular size is ~0.86°, corresponding to ℓ ≈ 220 in the power spectrum. The observed ℓ_1 = 220 ± 1 nails Ω_total = 1.000 ± 0.005 — pinning the universe as spatially flat at the percent level.

slides.prompt: You measure the deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio D/H in a high-redshift quasar absorption system (a primordial gas cloud) and find D/H = 2.5×10⁻⁵. What can you infer?

choices.label: The baryon density of the universe, independent of CMB measurements.
choices.rationale: Correct. D/H is the most sensitive primordial-abundance probe of baryon density because deuterium is fragile — burned in stellar interiors, never made there. D/H reflects exclusively BBN; higher Ω_b ⇒ faster D destruction by D+p→³He+γ ⇒ less D survives. D/H = 2.5×10⁻⁵ ⇒ Ω_b h² ≈ 0.022, matching CMB-derived value to within ~5%. This independent agreement is one of the strongest tests of ΛCDM + the Big Bang model.

choices.label: The Hubble constant H_0 directly.
choices.rationale: D/H doesn't constrain H_0 — it constrains Ω_b. H_0 comes from independent measurements.

choices.label: The neutrino mass.
choices.rationale: BBN constraints on N_eff (effective number of relativistic species) loosely bound neutrino properties, but D/H doesn't pin down ν masses directly.

choices.label: The total matter density Ω_m.
choices.rationale: Ω_m includes dark matter, which doesn't participate in BBN. D/H probes only the baryonic component Ω_b.

slides.hint: What makes D special among primordial isotopes?
slides.workedSolution: Deuterium is the most fragile primordial isotope: stellar nucleosynthesis destroys it (it's instantly burned via D+p→³He). So any D/H you measure in cosmologically pristine gas reflects BBN with no later contamination — making D/H the cleanest 'baryometer.' Theory: D/H ∝ (η_baryon)^(−1.6). Measurement: D/H = (2.5 ± 0.1)×10⁻⁵ in high-z DLAs ⇒ Ω_b h² = 0.0222 ± 0.0005. Planck CMB: Ω_b h² = 0.0224 ± 0.0001. Agreement at < 1σ between probes separated by 300,000 years and a vast difference in physics — a remarkable concordance test.

slides.prompt: A galaxy is observed at redshift z = 0.5. By what factor was the universe smaller (in linear scale) when its light was emitted? (Answer the ratio a_now / a_emit.)
slides.workedSolution: 1 + z = 1.5, so the universe was 1.5× smaller in linear extent at emission (i.e., a_emit = a_now / 1.5). Photon wavelengths have stretched by 50% en route. This is *not* a Doppler shift; it's the expansion of space itself.

slides.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain the 'big-bang model' to a curious 16-year-old. What evidence supports it? What are the most fundamental open questions?
rubric: Universe began ~13.8 Gyr ago in a hot, dense state; has expanded + cooled since.

Three pillars of evidence: (1) Hubble's law — galaxies recede with v=H_0 d; (2) CMB — 2.725 K blackbody relic from t=380 kyr; (3) BBN — light-element abundances (H, He, D, Li) match nuclear-rate calculations at t~1 sec.

Open questions: nature of dark matter (~27%); nature of dark energy (~68%, causes accelerated expansion); origin of initial perturbations (inflation? bounce? something stranger?); Hubble tension; matter-antimatter asymmetry.
Big Bang is not a 'beginning' question — it's a model from t > 10⁻³² s onward. What happened *at* t=0 is unknown.
